questions.q: A mobile app streams events to Kinesis Data Streams. The business needs per-user rolling metrics over 30 minutes, and events can arrive several minutes late but must be counted in the right window. Which service fits?

options.t: Lambda with a Kinesis event source mapping and tumbling windows
options.why: Wrong: Lambda windows are tumbling only, at most 15 minutes, with no event-time watermarks.

options.t: Amazon Data Firehose with a Lambda transform
options.why: Wrong: Firehose transforms per record; no windows over many records and no long-lived state.

options.t: Managed Service for Apache Flink with event-time windows and watermarks
options.why: Right: Flink keeps keyed state and uses watermarks to place late events in the correct window.

options.t: A KCL consumer on EC2 that checkpoints to DynamoDB
options.why: Wrong: possible, but you build windows, state and late-data logic yourself, with much more operations work.

questions.explain: Event time, watermarks and windows longer than 15 minutes point to Managed Service for Apache Flink.
questions.remember: Stateful windows, event time, late data, joins or exactly-once state on a stream → Managed Service for Apache Flink.
variants: Only a simple per-record transform is needed → Lambda.
Team already uses Spark and accepts seconds of latency → Glue streaming ETL.
Interactive SQL exploration of the stream → MSF Studio.

questions.q: A team must land a Kinesis data stream in S3 as Parquet files for Athena. There is no aggregation, joining or other stateful logic. They want the least code and cost. What should they use?

options.t: Amazon Data Firehose with format conversion to Parquet
options.why: Right: Firehose buffers and delivers to S3, converts to Parquet, and needs no code.

options.t: Managed Service for Apache Flink with a FileSink
options.why: Wrong: it works, but adds code and always-on KPU cost for no gain when there is no stateful logic.

options.t: Flink on Amazon EMR
options.why: Wrong: you also manage a cluster for a job that needs no Flink at all.

options.t: MSF Studio notebook writing to S3
options.why: Wrong: notebooks are for interactive work and bill extra KPUs while running.

questions.explain: Pure buffered delivery with format conversion is Firehose's job.
questions.remember: No-code delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch or Iceberg with buffering → Firehose. Add MSF only when you need windows, joins or state.
variants: The pipeline must also sessionize users before landing → MSF, then FileSink/Iceberg or Firehose.
Exactly-once file output is required → MSF FileSink (Firehose is at-least-once).

questions.q: An older design uses Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL with RANDOM_CUT_FOREST to flag anomalies in a sensor stream. The team is rebuilding it today. What is the correct approach?

options.t: Keep the KDA for SQL application and only upgrade its runtime
options.why: Wrong: KDA for SQL was shut down; its applications were deleted starting 27 January 2026.

options.t: Migrate in place to Managed Service for Apache Flink with no code change
options.why: Wrong: moving from KDA for SQL is a rewrite, not an upgrade.

options.t: Use Firehose with a RANDOM_CUT_FOREST transform setting
options.why: Wrong: Firehose has no such function and no state across records.

options.t: Rewrite in Managed Service for Apache Flink (app or Studio) with custom anomaly logic or a SageMaker endpoint call
options.why: Right: RANDOM_CUT_FOREST left with KDA for SQL; in Flink you build detection with keyed state, CEP, or Async I/O to SageMaker.

questions.explain: KDA for SQL no longer exists; Flink-based MSF replaces it with your own anomaly logic.
questions.remember: "Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL" in a modern scenario → not available; rewrite in MSF or MSF Studio. "KDA for Apache Flink" = MSF (renamed August 2023).
variants: A question names "Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink" → read it as Managed Service for Apache Flink.
Analysts only want ad hoc SQL on the live stream → MSF Studio.

questions.q: An MSF application is set to Parallelism 8 and ParallelismPerKPU 2. How many KPUs are billed per hour while it runs?

options.why: Wrong: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 KPUs for processing, but every application also pays one orchestration KPU.
Right: 4 processing KPUs plus 1 orchestration KPU.
Wrong: that ignores ParallelismPerKPU, which packs 2 subtasks per KPU.
Wrong: KPUs are Parallelism divided by ParallelismPerKPU, not multiplied.

questions.explain: Allocated KPUs = Parallelism ÷ ParallelismPerKPU (rounded up), plus 1 orchestration KPU.
questions.remember: KPUs = ceil(Parallelism ÷ ParallelismPerKPU) + 1 orchestration KPU. A KPU = 1 vCPU, 4 GB memory, 50 GB running storage. Billing is on allocated KPUs, not CPU used.
variants: It is a Studio notebook → 2 extra KPUs (orchestration + interactive environment) plus query KPUs.
The app is stopped (READY) → no KPU charge; snapshots still bill storage.
Smallest streaming app → 1 + 1 = 2 KPUs.

questions.q: An MSF job calls an external HTTP service for each record. CPU stays around 25%, but source lag keeps growing. Which change uses the KPUs most efficiently?

options.t: Lower ParallelismPerKPU to 1
options.why: Wrong: that gives each subtask a full vCPU it does not use; the job is waiting on I/O, not CPU.

options.t: Wait for built-in autoscaling to add KPUs
options.why: Wrong: autoscaling triggers only on containerCPUUtilization ≥ 75%, so a low-CPU job never scales.

options.t: Raise ParallelismPerKPU so more subtasks share each KPU
options.why: Right: I/O-bound subtasks spend time waiting, so more of them per vCPU raises throughput without wasting KPUs.

options.t: Move the job to Firehose
options.why: Wrong: Firehose cannot run this enrichment logic with state.

questions.explain: I/O-bound jobs pack well: raise ParallelismPerKPU (max 8).
questions.remember: I/O-bound (low CPU, waiting on calls) → raise ParallelismPerKPU. CPU- or memory-heavy → keep it at 1. Too high → less memory per subtask, network buffer errors or OOM.
variants: After raising it, a CPU-heavy job hits OOM → lower ParallelismPerKPU again.
The calls block the operator thread → also use Async I/O.

questions.q: A new MSF application starts at parallelism 16. The team expects to scale to parallelism 400 within a year and must keep state across scaling. What should they do now?

options.t: Set maxParallelism explicitly in code above the planned peak
options.why: Right: without it, maxParallelism defaults to 128, and changing it later breaks restore from older snapshots.

options.t: Nothing; autoscaling will raise maxParallelism when needed
options.why: Wrong: autoscaling never scales past maxParallelism.

options.t: Set Parallelism to 400 from day one
options.why: Wrong: you pay for 400 subtasks you do not need yet, and autoscaling never goes below the configured Parallelism.

options.t: Raise ParallelismPerKPU to 8
options.why: Wrong: it changes how subtasks pack into KPUs, not the key-group limit.

questions.explain: maxParallelism (key groups) caps scaling with state and defaults to 128 when the job starts at ≤ 128.
questions.remember: Plan to go above parallelism 128 while keeping state → set maxParallelism from day one. Changing it later means starting without a snapshot.
variants: Autoscaling stops at parallelism 128 → maxParallelism is the cap; raising it needs fresh state.
The app needs more than 64 KPUs → request a per-app KPU quota increase naming the app.

questions.q: An MSF app reads a Kinesis stream with 4 shards at parallelism 16. Deserialization of large JSON records is the bottleneck and 12 source subtasks are idle. What is the best fix without resharding?

options.t: Raise Parallelism to 32
options.why: Wrong: each shard is read by one subtask, so more source subtasks stay idle.

options.t: Enable enhanced fan-out
options.why: Wrong: EFO adds read throughput per shard; it does not spread the parsing work.

options.t: Use processing time instead of event time
options.why: Wrong: time semantics do not change how work is spread across subtasks.

options.t: Read raw bytes at the source, rebalance(), then deserialize in a wider downstream operator
options.why: Right: rebalance spreads records round robin to all subtasks so the heavy parsing uses all 16.

questions.explain: Source parallelism is capped by shards; move heavy work after a rebalance.
questions.remember: Shards (Kinesis) or partitions (Kafka) cap source parallelism. Heavy per-record work → read bytes, rebalance(), process wider downstream.
variants: The stream can be resharded → add shards and pass the new count as a runtime property.
Skew comes from one hot key, not few shards → better key or salting.

questions.q: Analysts explored a live Kinesis stream in an MSF Studio notebook with Flink SQL. The query must now run 24/7, keep durable state and be able to scale. What should they do?

options.t: Leave the notebook running
options.why: Wrong: notebooks do not autoscale, checkpoints are off by default, and the notebook bills 2 extra KPUs.

options.t: Deploy the note as an application with durable state
options.why: Right: it builds the note into code in S3 and creates a normal streaming MSF app with snapshots and autoscaling.

options.t: Recreate the query in Kinesis Data Analytics for SQL
options.why: Wrong: KDA for SQL was shut down.

options.t: Schedule the notebook with EventBridge Scheduler
options.why: Wrong: it is still an interactive notebook without durable state.

questions.explain: Studio is for exploration; production runs as a deployed MSF application.
questions.remember: Interactive SQL on a stream → MSF Studio (Zeppelin, needs a Glue Data Catalog database). Must run continuously → deploy as application with durable state.
variants: A deployed note fails on a plain SELECT → change it to INSERT INTO a sink table.
The user wants Flink 2.2 features in Studio → not possible; Studio stays on 1.x runtimes.

questions.q: An MSF app shows downtime > 0 and a rising restart count. Logs show RUNNING → FAILED each time on the same malformed record. What fixes it?

options.t: Scale up KPUs
options.why: Wrong: more capacity does not help; the same record replays after each restart.

options.t: Turn off checkpointing
options.why: Wrong: restarts would then lose state and position, and the record would still fail.

options.t: Catch the exception in the operator and send the bad record to a side output (dead-letter path)
options.why: Right: the poison record is removed from the main flow and the job keeps running.

options.t: Restart from the latest snapshot
options.why: Wrong: the snapshot's source position is before the bad record, so it fails again.

questions.explain: A poison record causes an endless restart loop; handle it in code.
questions.remember: Restart loop on the same record (poison pill) → catch exceptions, route bad records to a side output/DLQ. Lag rising + restarts → fix the crash before scaling.
variants: Restart loop right after an update → incompatible state or operator ID mismatch: UIDs, AllowNonRestoredState, SKIP_RESTORE_FROM_SNAPSHOT or roll back.
TaskManager heartbeat timeouts → CPU/memory pressure: more KPUs or lower ParallelismPerKPU.

questions.q: A team will do an in-place upgrade of a production MSF app from Flink 1.20 to 2.2. Which TWO steps best protect them if the new version fails? (Choose 2)

options.t: Delete the app and recreate it with the new runtime
options.why: Wrong: that loses snapshots; in-place upgrade keeps the same ARN, snapshots, logs and settings.

options.t: Take a snapshot (or keep automatic snapshots on) before the upgrade
options.why: Right: rollback needs a pre-upgrade snapshot, and 2.x state cannot be restored on 1.x.

options.t: Turn off snapshots during the upgrade
options.why: Wrong: without snapshots, updates lose state.

options.t: Turn on system rollback before upgrading
options.why: Right: if binary incompatibilities stop the job starting, MSF rolls back without you.

questions.explain: Snapshot first and enable system rollback; use RollbackApplication for a restart loop that appears after start.
questions.remember: Before any risky update: named snapshot, system rollback on, UIDs set. 1.x → 2.x is one-way for state; going back uses the pre-upgrade 1.x snapshot.
variants: Upgrade "succeeded" but the job restart-loops → RollbackApplication manually.
Upgrade succeeded but app is on the old runtime → a system rollback happened; check ListApplicationOperations.
The app is a Studio notebook → in-place version upgrades are not supported.

questions.q: An MSF app restarts now and then, but the team sees no useful errors in CloudWatch Logs. The monitoring log level is ERROR. What should they change?

options.t: Set the log level to INFO
options.why: Right: AWS recommends INFO because many Flink errors are logged at INFO, not ERROR.

options.t: Set the log level to DEBUG permanently
options.why: Wrong: DEBUG significantly slows the app; use it only temporarily.

options.t: Log every record in the operators
options.why: Wrong: that causes bottlenecks and backpressure.

options.t: Look in CloudTrail for the failures
options.why: Wrong: CloudTrail records management API calls, not per-record processing errors.

questions.explain: INFO is the recommended level; ERROR hides many Flink errors.
questions.remember: Log level INFO for production, DEBUG only briefly, never log every record. CloudTrail = who called StartApplication/StopApplication; app logs = processing errors.
variants: Logs do not appear at all → check role permissions on the log stream (logs:PutLogEvents) and that the app is running.
Auditors ask who stopped the app → CloudTrail StopApplication event.
Logs might contain PII → remove it; MSF cannot encrypt app logs with a CMK.

questions.q: A dashboard must show the average order value for the last 10 minutes, refreshed every minute. Which Flink window fits?

options.t: Tumbling window of 10 minutes
options.why: Wrong: tumbling windows do not overlap, so the value refreshes only every 10 minutes.

options.t: Session window with a 10-minute gap
options.why: Wrong: session windows close after inactivity and vary in length.

options.t: Global window with a count trigger
options.why: Wrong: it fires on record counts, not on a time schedule.

options.t: Sliding (hop) window of 10 minutes sliding every 1 minute
options.why: Right: windows overlap, so a new 10-minute result comes out every minute.

questions.explain: Overlapping "last N, updated every M" = sliding window.
questions.remember: Tumbling = fixed, no overlap; sliding = overlapping (each event in size ÷ slide windows); session = gap of inactivity; cumulate = running total in steps.
variants: Web sessions ending after 30 minutes of inactivity → session window with a 30-minute gap.
Running daily total updated each hour → CUMULATE window TVF.
Rolling average per row → SQL OVER window.

questions.q: A retail team wants a running total of sales for the current day, updated every hour, written with Flink SQL. Which window is designed for this?

options.t: TUMBLE with a 1-hour size
options.why: Wrong: it gives each hour's total, not a total growing through the day.

options.t: CUMULATE with a 1-hour step and 1-day max size
options.why: Right: the window grows in steps inside one day and emits the running total each hour.

options.t: HOP of 1 day sliding every hour
options.why: Wrong: it gives the last 24 hours, not the current calendar day, and copies each event 24 times.

options.t: windowAll over the whole stream
options.why: Wrong: non-keyed windows run at parallelism 1 and are a bottleneck.

questions.explain: A running total that grows in steps inside a fixed max size is a CUMULATE window.
questions.remember: Grows in steps inside one period → CUMULATE. Fixed buckets → TUMBLE. Last N refreshed every M → HOP.
variants: Hourly totals only → TUMBLE of 1 hour.
Top 3 products per minute → tumbling window aggregate + window Top-N (ROW_NUMBER ≤ N).

questions.q: An MSF job reads a Kinesis stream. Some shards get no data at night, and from then on the event-time windows downstream never fire, even though other shards carry traffic. What is the fix?

options.t: Switch the source reader to enhanced fan-out
options.why: Wrong: EFO raises read throughput; it does not change watermarks.

options.t: Lower the out-of-orderness bound
options.why: Wrong: the problem is a stuck minimum watermark, not the bound.

options.t: Configure withIdleness on the watermark strategy
options.why: Right: idle inputs are excluded from the minimum watermark after that time, so windows fire again.

options.t: Increase the checkpoint interval
options.why: Wrong: checkpoints do not drive window firing.

questions.explain: Idle shards send no watermark and hold back the minimum; withIdleness excludes them.
questions.remember: Event-time windows never fire + quiet shards/partitions → withIdleness (and uniformShardAssigner). If all inputs are idle, time still does not move forward.
variants: Too many records dropped as late → larger out-of-orderness bound, allowed lateness or a late-data side output.
The very last window in a test never closes → send one more event or a heartbeat.

questions.q: Orders and payments arrive on two streams. Each order must be matched with its payment if it arrives within 1 hour, and state must not grow forever. Which join should be used?

options.t: Interval join on order ID with a 1-hour bound
options.why: Right: it keeps only records inside the interval, cleans state as the watermark moves, and outputs append-only rows.

options.t: Regular SQL join on order ID
options.why: Wrong: both sides are kept in state forever unless you add TTL.

options.t: Lookup join against a JDBC table
options.why: Wrong: it queries an external table, not a second stream.

options.t: Broadcast state join
options.why: Wrong: it is for small reference data that fits on every subtask, not a large payment stream.

questions.explain: Two time-related streams → interval join.
questions.remember: Time-related streams → interval join; value as of event time → temporal join; external DB enrichment → lookup join or Async I/O; small rules table → broadcast state.
variants: A regular join's state grows forever → set table.exec.state.ttl or switch to an interval join.
Impression + click within 30 minutes → interval join.

questions.q: Each order event must be enriched with the currency exchange rate that was valid at the order's event time, even when old orders are replayed. Rates arrive as a changelog keyed by currency. Which join gives correct results?

options.t: Lookup join on the rates database
options.why: Wrong: a lookup join returns the current value at processing time, not the historic rate.

options.t: Regular join on currency
options.why: Wrong: it keeps everything forever and does not pick the version valid at order time.

options.t: Window join in a 1-minute tumbling window
options.why: Wrong: it only matches records that land in the same window.

options.t: Temporal join FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF the order time on a versioned rate table
options.why: Right: it joins each order with the rate version valid at the order's event time.

questions.explain: "Value as of the event's time" = temporal join on a versioned table (primary key + event time).
questions.remember: Historic-correct enrichment → temporal join (versioned table, e.g. upsert-kafka or CDC). Current value from a DB → lookup join with cache.
variants: Each event needs the current customer tier from RDS → lookup join (or Async I/O) with a lookup cache.
Rules change at runtime without redeploy → broadcast state from a rules stream.

questions.q: An MSF app's lastCheckpointSize has grown every week for months, although traffic is flat. Which TWO are likely causes? (Choose 2)

options.t: A regular SQL join or GROUP BY on user IDs with no state TTL
options.why: Right: unbounded keys with no TTL keep state forever.

options.t: Checkpoints use incremental mode
options.why: Wrong: incremental checkpoints upload only changed files; they do not cause growth.

options.t: A week-long window using ProcessWindowFunction
options.why: Right: ProcessWindowFunction keeps every event in state; use incremental aggregation instead.

options.t: Operators have .uid() set
options.why: Wrong: UIDs only map state to operators on restore.

questions.explain: State leaks come from missing TTL on unbounded keys and from long windows that buffer every event.
questions.remember: Checkpoint size growing with flat traffic → state leak: add state TTL, use AggregateFunction/ReduceFunction, prefer interval joins. TTL shrinks size only after RocksDB compaction (or in a snapshot).
variants: TTL is set but checkpoint size has not dropped → wait for RocksDB compaction or take a snapshot.
Duplicates must be removed within 24 hours → keyed "seen" state with a 24-hour TTL.

questions.q: A Flink SQL job runs SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM clicks GROUP BY user_id with no window, and the write to a Kinesis Data Streams sink fails. Why, and what is the fix?

options.t: Kinesis records are too large; compress them
options.why: Wrong: the problem is the kind of result, not record size.

options.t: The result is an updating changelog; window the aggregate or write to an upsert-capable sink
options.why: Right: a plain GROUP BY emits updates, and append-only sinks like Kinesis reject them.

options.t: The job lacks a watermark; add one
options.why: Wrong: without a window the result still updates on every record.

options.t: The Kinesis sink needs EFO
options.why: Wrong: EFO is a source reader setting.

questions.explain: Non-windowed GROUP BY produces updates; append-only sinks cannot take them.
questions.remember: Updating (changelog) results need upsert sinks (upsert-kafka, JDBC with primary key, DynamoDB, Iceberg v2). Append-only sinks (Kinesis, plain files) need windowed or filter-only queries.
variants: The same query with a tumbling window → append-only, Kinesis sink works.
EXPLAIN shows the plan and reveals unwanted updating results.

questions.q: After a developer added a stateless map step to an MSF job, the update fails to restore from the snapshot with an operator ID mismatch. What prevents this in the future?

options.t: Turn off automatic snapshots
options.why: Wrong: updates would then lose all state.

options.t: Raise maxParallelism
options.why: Wrong: changing maxParallelism also breaks restore.

options.t: Set a unique .uid() on every stateful operator
options.why: Right: state is matched by operator ID; generated IDs change when the job graph changes.

options.t: Use the HashMap state backend
options.why: Wrong: the backend does not fix ID matching, and MSF uses RocksDB.

questions.explain: Stable operator UIDs keep snapshot restore working across code changes.
questions.remember: Set .uid() (and .name()) on every stateful operator. Added operator → fine; removed operator → AllowNonRestoredState=true; incompatible state → SKIP_RESTORE_FROM_SNAPSHOT or fix code.
variants: A stateful operator was deleted and the app will not start → AllowNonRestoredState=true.
State uses Kryo before a Flink 2.2 upgrade → move to Avro/POJO or test, since Kryo 5.6 may not read old state.

questions.q: An MSF job enriches each event with a synchronous DynamoDB GetItem call. The enrichment operator is slow and upstream operators are backpressured. What is the best fix?

options.t: Use Async I/O for the DynamoDB calls
options.why: Right: it calls external services without blocking the operator thread, with a timeout and capacity limit.

options.t: Use processing time instead of event time
options.why: Wrong: time semantics do not affect blocking calls.

options.t: Lower ParallelismPerKPU to 1
options.why: Wrong: gives more CPU, but the thread still sits blocked on each call.

options.t: Add withIdleness to the watermark strategy
options.why: Wrong: it fixes stuck watermarks, not slow I/O.

questions.explain: Blocking enrichment calls cause backpressure; Async I/O removes the block.
questions.remember: External lookups per event → Async I/O (unordered for lower latency, ordered to keep order) or a SQL lookup join with cache.
variants: The slow operator is a sink → scale the sink target (shards, WCU) or raise parallelism.
Backpressure reading rule: the slow operator is just downstream of the last highly backpressured one.

questions.q: A developer set a 10-second checkpoint interval in the Flink code, but the app still checkpoints every 60 seconds. What is the cause?

options.t: The app has too few KPUs
options.why: Wrong: capacity does not reset the interval.

options.t: Snapshots are disabled
options.why: Wrong: snapshots are separate from periodic checkpoints.

options.t: MinPauseBetweenCheckpoints is 60 seconds
options.why: Wrong: the default minimum pause is 5,000 ms.

options.t: The checkpoint configuration is ConfigurationType=DEFAULT, which overrides code values
options.why: Right: with DEFAULT, the service defaults (on, 60,000 ms, 5,000 ms min pause) win; set CUSTOM to change them.

questions.explain: DEFAULT checkpoint configuration ignores values from code; use CUSTOM.
questions.remember: MSF checkpoint defaults: enabled, 60 s interval, 5 s min pause. To change them set ConfigurationType=CUSTOM. Shorter interval = less reprocessing but more overhead and small files.
variants: Parquet files on S3 are tiny → lengthen the interval, since bulk formats roll on every checkpoint.
Kafka exactly-once data appears late → latency equals the checkpoint interval.

questions.q: A code bug corrupted results starting at 10:00. The team has scheduled named snapshots several times a day. They deploy a fixed version. How do they reprocess from before the bug while keeping earlier state?

options.t: Start with SKIP_RESTORE_FROM_SNAPSHOT
options.why: Wrong: that throws away all state from before 10:00.

options.t: Start with RESTORE_FROM_CUSTOM_SNAPSHOT naming a snapshot taken before 10:00
options.why: Right: the snapshot restores state and source positions, so records after it are reprocessed.

options.t: Restore a specific checkpoint by name
options.why: Wrong: checkpoints are service-owned; you cannot list or restore one by name.

options.t: Restart with the source at LATEST
options.why: Wrong: it skips the affected data instead of reprocessing it.

questions.explain: Named snapshots are point-in-time restore points; replay depends on source retention.
questions.remember: Rewind = RESTORE_FROM_CUSTOM_SNAPSHOT + SnapshotName. Schedule snapshots (EventBridge Scheduler) and delete old ones (limit 1,000 per app; MSF never deletes them). Sinks must tolerate the replay.
variants: Manual snapshots fail with LimitExceededException → delete old snapshots.
No snapshot fits and state is not needed → start without snapshot at AT_TIMESTAMP, with source retention covering the gap.

questions.q: An MSF app reads from MSK and writes to another Kafka topic. Downstream consumers must see each result exactly once, even after failures. Which TWO settings are required? (Choose 2)

options.t: KafkaSink with DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE and a transactionalIdPrefix
options.why: Right: writes go into Kafka transactions committed when the checkpoint completes.

options.t: Commit source offsets back to Kafka after each record
options.why: Wrong: offsets live in Flink checkpoints; committing to Kafka is only for monitoring.

options.t: Disable checkpointing to reduce latency
options.why: Wrong: transactions commit on checkpoints, so exactly-once needs them.

options.t: Downstream consumers use isolation.level=read_committed
options.why: Right: otherwise they read uncommitted or aborted data.

questions.explain: End-to-end exactly-once = replayable source + checkpointed state + transactional or idempotent sink.
questions.remember: Exactly-once to Kafka → EXACTLY_ONCE KafkaSink + read_committed consumers; transaction timeout > checkpoint interval + restart time, and ≤ broker transaction.max.timeout.ms (15 min default).
variants: Output to Kinesis Data Streams → at-least-once; dedupe downstream by event ID.
Output to S3 → FileSink or Iceberg sink commit on checkpoint (exactly-once).

questions.q: An MSF FileSink writes Parquet to S3 with parallelism 32 and many date/hour partitions. Athena queries are slow because of thousands of tiny files. Which change helps most?

options.t: Switch to a row format such as JSON
options.why: Wrong: it loses columnar benefits for Athena.

options.t: Shorten the checkpoint interval
options.why: Wrong: bulk formats roll on every checkpoint, so this makes even more files.

options.t: Lengthen the checkpoint interval or lower the sink parallelism (and compact later)
options.why: Right: fewer rolls and fewer writers give larger files.

options.t: Turn off checkpointing
options.why: Wrong: FileSink finishes files only on checkpoint, so files would never be finished.

questions.explain: Parquet/ORC files roll on every checkpoint; interval × parallelism × partitions sets file count.
questions.remember: Small files from MSF → longer checkpoint interval, lower sink parallelism, or compaction. Iceberg sink: one commit per checkpoint → run compaction and snapshot expiry.
variants: Readers see half-written data → read only finished files; in-progress and pending files are hidden by prefix.
Iceberg tables gather thousands of snapshots a day → enable table optimizers or S3 Tables maintenance.

questions.q: An MSF app with autoscaling on shows rising millisBehindLatest. CPU (containerCPUUtilization) is steady at 30% because the job waits on a slow sink. What should the team do?

options.t: Wait; autoscaling will add KPUs once lag passes its threshold
options.why: Wrong: built-in autoscaling watches only CPU (≥ 75% for 15 minutes); lag does not trigger it.

options.t: Build custom scaling from a CloudWatch alarm on millisBehindLatest that calls UpdateApplication, or raise ParallelismPerKPU
options.why: Right: CPU-based autoscaling never fires for an I/O-bound job, so scale on lag or pack more subtasks per KPU.

options.t: Lower the checkpoint interval
options.why: Wrong: that adds overhead and does not speed the sink.

options.t: Disable autoscaling and set ParallelismPerKPU to 1
options.why: Wrong: gives more CPU to a job that is not CPU-bound.

questions.explain: Only CPU triggers built-in autoscaling.
questions.remember: Autoscaling: up when containerCPU ≥ 75% for 15 min (×2), down when < 10% for 6 h (÷2); never below configured Parallelism or above KPU limit/maxParallelism; each scale restarts the job.
variants: CPU at 90% for 20 minutes → autoscaling doubles parallelism.
Predictable 9:00 peak → scheduled scaling before 9:00.
Bill doubled after a short spike → scale-down waits 6 hours under 10% CPU.

questions.q: Two MSF applications and a Lambda function all poll the same Kinesis stream. The MSF apps log ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded and lag grows, though the stream is not near its write limit. What is the best fix?

options.t: Raise Parallelism on both MSF apps
options.why: Wrong: more readers on shared polling make throttling worse.

options.t: Switch both apps to processing time
options.why: Wrong: time semantics do not affect read limits.

options.t: Set the source start position to TRIM_HORIZON
options.why: Wrong: it changes where reading starts, not read throughput.

options.t: Use enhanced fan-out (READER_TYPE=EFO) with a unique consumer name per app
options.why: Right: each EFO consumer gets its own 2 MB/s per shard instead of sharing 2 MB/s and 5 reads/s.

questions.explain: Polling consumers share each shard's read limit; EFO gives dedicated throughput.
questions.remember: Read throttling from many consumers → EFO (unique EFO_CONSUMER_NAME per stream), or fewer records per call/longer interval. EFO costs extra; use it only when needed.
variants: Write throttling on the output stream → more shards/on-demand or a better partition key.
Least-privilege role with EFO → SELF_MANAGED lifecycle, so the role needs no register/deregister permissions.

questions.q: A new MSF application must process the 3 days of data already in its Kinesis stream before continuing with live data. It has never run before. How should the source be configured?

options.t: Start position TRIM_HORIZON (or AT_TIMESTAMP) and start without a snapshot
options.why: Right: the default is LATEST, which skips everything written before the app started.

options.t: Leave the default start position
options.why: Wrong: the default LATEST reads only new records.

options.t: Enable enhanced fan-out
options.why: Wrong: EFO changes throughput, not where reading starts.

options.t: Restore from the latest snapshot
options.why: Wrong: a new app has no snapshot, and a snapshot would resume from its saved position anyway.

questions.explain: Kinesis source default is LATEST; set TRIM_HORIZON or AT_TIMESTAMP to read older data.
questions.remember: Reprocess history → start without snapshot at TRIM_HORIZON/AT_TIMESTAMP (Kafka: earliest/timestamp offsets). Replay is limited by source retention (KDS 24 h default, up to 365 days).
variants: Must reprocess the last 7 days → KDS retention must be at least 7 days.
Early watermarks when catching up from TRIM_HORIZON → add an out-of-orderness buffer or allowed lateness.

questions.q: A CDC stream from Kafka must be upserted into a transactional data lake table on S3 that Athena queries, with exactly-once results. Which design fits?

options.t: MSF writing JSON files with FileSink to S3
options.why: Wrong: append-only files keep every change, not the latest row per key.

options.t: Firehose delivering to S3 with Lambda transforms
options.why: Wrong: Firehose is at-least-once and has no per-key state.

options.t: MSF writing to an Iceberg v2 table (Glue Data Catalog or S3 Tables), plus compaction and snapshot expiry
options.why: Right: the Iceberg sink commits on each checkpoint (exactly-once) and v2 supports upserts.

options.t: MSF writing to a Kinesis Data Streams sink
options.why: Wrong: at-least-once, and not a data lake table.

questions.explain: Streaming ETL into a transactional lake with exactly-once → MSF → Iceberg.
questions.remember: MSF → Iceberg v2 for exactly-once upserts into a lake; one commit per checkpoint, so run compaction. Role needs S3 and Glue permissions, and the Glue database must exist.
variants: CDC kept as latest value per key in Kafka → upsert-kafka.
Producers change record formats often → Glue Schema Registry with compatibility rules.

questions.q: An MSF app was attached to private subnets so it could read MSK. Since then its DynamoDB sink fails with timeouts. Which fix is most cost-effective?

options.t: Move the app into public subnets
options.why: Wrong: the app ENIs get no public IP, so public subnets do not give internet access.

options.t: Add a DynamoDB gateway VPC endpoint to the private subnets' route tables
options.why: Right: VPC-attached apps lose default internet access, and a gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB without NAT data charges.

options.t: Remove the VPC configuration
options.why: Wrong: the app would lose access to the private MSK cluster.

options.t: Add the DynamoDB permissions to the KMS key policy
options.why: Wrong: this is a network path problem, not a permission problem.

questions.explain: VPC-attached MSF apps need a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to reach AWS APIs.
questions.remember: VPC config → ENIs in your subnets, no internet unless the VPC gives it: private subnets + NAT or VPC endpoints (S3/DynamoDB gateway; Kinesis, Logs, KMS, STS, Secrets Manager interface). Durable state needs no endpoint.
variants: App cannot reach MSK at all → VPC-configure the app and allow the app's security group inbound on the broker SG.
Subnets run out of IPs during scale-out → ENI count grows with parallelism; use larger subnets.

questions.q: A security team wants an MSF app's checkpoints and snapshots encrypted with their own KMS key, and that key must be usable only by that one application. What should they do?

options.t: Use the default encryption
options.why: Wrong: default encryption uses AWS owned keys, not the team's key.

options.t: Use an asymmetric customer managed key
options.why: Wrong: MSF supports symmetric KMS keys only.

options.t: Set an S3 bucket policy on the durable storage bucket
options.why: Wrong: the durable storage bucket is service-managed and not visible to you.

options.t: Set a symmetric customer managed key on the app, with a key policy condition on kms:EncryptionContext:aws:kinesisanalytics:arn equal to the app ARN
options.why: Right: MSF sends the app ARN as encryption context, so the condition limits the key to that app.

questions.explain: CMK for MSF state is symmetric only; encryption context aws:kinesisanalytics:arn ties it to one app.
questions.remember: CMK covers running and durable storage (checkpoints/snapshots). It does not cover sources/sinks, app logs or old snapshots. After key rotation, stop and start the app. The API caller also needs key permissions.
variants: The key was rotated → stop and start so running storage uses new key material.
Sources and sinks must be encrypted → configure KDS SSE-KMS or S3 SSE-KMS on those services.

questions.q: A CI/CD role gets AccessDenied when calling CreateApplication for an MSF app that uses an existing service execution role. The role already has kinesisanalytics:CreateApplication. What is missing?

options.t: iam:PassRole on the service execution role
options.why: Right: the caller passes the execution role to the service and needs iam:PassRole for it.

options.t: kinesisanalytics:* in the service execution role
options.why: Wrong: the execution role is not used for management calls; do not put lifecycle permissions there.

options.t: A resource-based policy on the MSF application
options.why: Wrong: MSF does not support resource-based policies on applications.

options.t: sts:AssumeRole for kinesis.amazonaws.com in the trust policy
options.why: Wrong: the trust principal is kinesisanalytics.amazonaws.com, and the error is on the caller side.

questions.explain: Creating or updating an app with a role needs iam:PassRole on that role.
questions.remember: Two kinds of permissions: management (caller's identity policy, kinesisanalytics:* actions + iam:PassRole) and application (the service execution role trusted by kinesisanalytics.amazonaws.com).
variants: One execution role reused by many apps → add aws:SourceArn/aws:SourceAccount to its trust policy (confused deputy).
Many teams share one account → ABAC on aws:ResourceTag and name-prefix ARNs.
The app needs a database password → Secrets Manager with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, never runtime properties.

questions.q: An MSF app's monthly bill roughly doubled after a short traffic spike. The spike lasted 20 minutes, and traffic has been normal for 3 hours since. What explains this, and what reduces cost for future spikes?

options.t: A KMS charge for checkpoints; switch to AWS owned keys
options.why: Wrong: KMS requests are a small separate cost and do not double KPU billing.

options.t: Autoscaling doubled KPUs and has not scaled down, since scale-down needs CPU under 10% for 6 hours; consider scheduled or custom scaling, and set the base Parallelism to normal load
options.why: Right: one CPU spike doubles parallelism and the larger size is billed for at least 6 hours.

options.t: The orchestration KPU was billed twice
options.why: Wrong: every app pays exactly one orchestration KPU.

options.t: Snapshots are billed as KPU-hours
options.why: Wrong: snapshots bill as durable backup storage per GB-month.

questions.explain: Billing follows allocated KPUs; autoscaling doubles fast and halves only after 6 quiet hours.
questions.remember: MSF cost = allocated KPU-hours (+1 orchestration KPU per app, +2 per Studio notebook) + running storage + snapshots. Stop apps (READY bills no KPUs), delete old snapshots, right-size Parallelism.
variants: A Studio notebook was left running all weekend → it billed at least 3 KPUs per hour.
A nightly 10-minute batch job → stop the app between runs.
Many small pipelines → each app pays its own orchestration KPU.
